title: Brooklyn concert hall said it was 'human made,' but site had AI flubs
excerpt: A new concert hall in Williamsburg, Brooklyn was briefly filled with AI-generated nostalgia for the neighborhood's artsy past.
content_html:
An upcoming music venue's AI flubs tell the story of a changing hipster neighborhood in Brooklyn

By Henry Chandonnet

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

and Sydney Bradley

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-22T10:36:01.288Z

The New York City concert hall Domino, set to open next year, is leaning into ye olde hipster days of Williamsburg. The AI flubs that permeated its website, though, were pure 2026.

Domino is founded by stomp-clapper Ben Lovett of Mumford & Sons, and its website included references to The Strokes and warehouse parties.

The AI-generated graphics on Domino's website included a ticket for a Strokes concert that never happened, blurry text and typos, and an artificial texture added on top that gave everything a nostalgic feel.

Ironically, smack dab in the middle of the site was a postcard with the text: "Human Made."

After Business Insider flagged the errors to Domino, a representative said that the site's designers ran out of time on the venue announcement and used AI as an "interim tool" until their "hand-made" version was complete.

"That falls short of what Domino stands for and we have replaced the website with something completely human made," they wrote.

Marketers are hotly debating when and where to use AI. Too much and you'll end up with oozing food, embarrassing typos — and a whole lot of angry Instagram comments. The Domino site's AI errors were especially noteworthy, given what they attempted to represent: a history of human creativity and musicmaking.

The site also serves as a curious proxy for what's happening in the neighborhood overall. AI has boomed in Williamsburg — the building where Domino will be based hosts several AI startups — and has sometimes awkwardly blended with the neighborhood's artsy tradition.

A change in the neighborhood

The Domino venue will be on the ground floor of The Refinery at Domino, a renovated office building where 75% of the occupants are tech companies — many of which are AI startups. Ads for OpenAI and Polymarket surround the building. It sits across from a padel court, a sport popular among the tech set.

TVG, Lovett's hospitality group behind the venue, is also backed by tech founders like Slack's Stewart Butterfield and Airbnb's Joe Gebbia.

It reflects a broader shift: Williamsburgians are attempting to marry tech and art — the engineers of the present and the creatives that defined its past.

When Business Insider wrote about the new "tech bro-hemia" forming in the neighborhood, readers shared their longing for a prior day. One told tech transplants to "go back to Cali."

Williamsburg's early-aughts aura had been dissipating for years before the AI boom, though, as the neighborhood's rents rose. The concert hall, which will open in 2027, aims to revive that grungy, artistic spirit in some form.

The Domino representative told Business Insider that the concert hall wanted to "honor the venues that shaped the Brooklyn music scene," like Glasslands and the Music Hall of Williamsburg. The former venue shuttered over a decade ago; the latter is set to close by the end of the year.

"The ethos of Domino is a celebration of all that is human made," the representative said.
